section_summary: This section covers diplomatic, political, economic, and military developments concerning Japan from August through December 1933, primarily recorded in U.S. Embassy Tokyo monthly reports (Despatches No. 510, 541, and 580) and Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda. Major diplomatic topics include the appointment of Koki Hirota as Foreign Minister, Japanese reaction to American naval expansion and Soviet-American rapprochement, negotiations over the Chinese Eastern Railway, and contentious Indo-Japanese cotton and tariff discussions at the Simla Conference. Domestically, the documents chronicle the trials and sentencing of the May 15 military and civilian assassins, the uncovering of the 'God-Sent Troops' coup plot, the revision of the Naval General Staff Ordinance, mounting budget controversies over defense expenditures, and fierce price wars in the domestic oil market driven by imports of Soviet gasoline.

subfiles.about: Monthly political report reviewing Japanese domestic politics, diplomacy, military preparations, and economic conditions for August 1933.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 510 transmits the Embassy's detailed review of developments in Japan during August 1933. Diplomatic sections cover Japanese apprehension over the American naval building program, the transit of T.V. Soong, negotiations for the purchase of the Chinese Eastern Railway, settlement of the Kamchatka fishery incident, and French claims to the Shonan Islands. Domestically, it recounts political party manoeuvres to influence the Saito Cabinet, the trials of the May 15 incident cadets and naval officers, air defense manoeuvres over Tokyo-Yokohama, and preliminary budget struggles for fiscal year 1934-1935. In economic affairs, it highlights expanding textile exports, gold market reactions to U.S. policy, and severe disruption of the domestic gasoline trade caused by Kojiro Matsukata's sales of Soviet petroleum.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 510: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of August, 1933

subfiles.about: State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing the Embassy's monthly report for September 1933.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman reviews key observations from Tokyo's September report, noting Japanese assumptions regarding early U.S. recognition of Soviet Russia and the moderating influence of newly appointed Foreign Minister Koki Hirota. The memorandum analyzes the implications of the American wheat and cotton loan to China and the dynamics of the Indo-Japanese trade talks at Simla, pointing out Japan's heavy shift to American cotton purchases. It also comments on the trials of civil and military terrorists, the reorganization of the Japanese Naval General Staff, government financing of naval replenishment and communications programs, and warnings given by the Foreign Office to foreign oil companies operating in Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo's Political Report for September 1933

subfiles.about: Monthly report and covering despatch detailing Japanese political, diplomatic, military, and commercial affairs during September 1933.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 541 forwards Report No. 84 on September 1933, emphasizing the assumption of the Foreign Affairs portfolio by Koki Hirota following Count Uchida's resignation and its favorable impact on foreign relations. The report surveys Japanese attitudes toward U.S. naval plans, the revolution in Cuba, and the American cotton loan to China, alongside the opening of the Simla trade conference and the diplomatic crisis surrounding arrests on the Chinese Eastern Railway. Domestic coverage centers on the four-year prison sentences given to Army cadets and procurator demands for capital punishment in the naval trial of the May 15 incident, the sensational 'God-Sent Troops' plot, and the revision of the Naval General Staff Ordinance granting strategic independence to the Chief of Staff. Economic developments examined include debates over a record budget of 2.8 billion yen, yen exchange strength, the price war between foreign oil distributors and Matsukata's Soviet gasoline, and reported Japanese agricultural concessions in Ethiopia.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 541: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of September, 1933

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on Japan for October 1933.
subfiles.summary: This memorandum provides an executive summary of Tokyo's monthly report for October 1933 transmitted in Despatch No. 580. It covers the shelving of a Japanese goodwill mission to the United States, speculation over Shigeru Yoshida replacing Katsuji Debuchi as Ambassador to Washington, and Japanese views on imminent U.S. recognition of the Soviet Union. On imperial trade, it details the deadlock at the Simla conference over Indian textile quotas, evidence of an effective Japanese boycott of Indian raw cotton, and a burgeoning tariff dispute with Australia over wool. In Manchukuo, it discusses the cartelization of four key industries, military control of amalgamated railways, the continuing impasse over the Chinese Eastern Railway, and a notable abatement of Soviet-Japanese border tensions.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo's Monthly Report for October 1933

subfiles.about: Cover despatch transmitting the Embassy's monthly report on conditions in Japan for October 1933.
subfiles.summary: In Despatch No. 580, Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits to the Secretary of State the Embassy's monthly report (Report No. 85) on political, economic, and social conditions in Japan for the month of October 1933 pursuant to standing Department instructions. Copies of the despatch and report are designated for distribution to diplomatic and consular posts in Peiping, Shanghai, Mukden, Harbin, and Dairen.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 580: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of October, 1933
